newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman stock market set for further gains -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Oman stock market set for further gains -analysts.

text.p: Confidence is running high on Oman's stock market, where a flood of money into the market looks set to drive prices even higher, analysts said on Tuesday.

Daily turnover on the Muscat Securities Market (MSM) has soared to around 4.4 million rials ($11.7 million) a day in the first five months of 1997 as the money has poured in, from some 787,000 rials a day in the same period in 1996, brokers said.
The market, which has over 100 stocks and is capitalised at around $5 billion, has risen a hefty 60 percent so far this year.

"Last year you would have seen about 20 people on the mezzanine above the trading floor. Now you see about 200 people there every day," Gulf Investment Services fund manager Bharath Rajnarayan told Reuters by telephone from Muscat.
The buying frenzy had pushed the index of some 50 blue chips to 320.53 points at the close on Tuesday from 200.34 points in early January.
"There is a lot of money which came into the market that was in real estate and other investments. Money invested abroad was also liquidated and has been moving in," Rajnarayan said.

"New investors are constantly entering the market. People are selling houses and land and coming to the market. Every day we see new investors," Financial Services Co general manager Waleed Nasser said, adding interest was also strong from the United Arab Emirates, which does not have an official floor.
Oman is the Gulf's most open economy with many listed firms allowing 49 percent foreign ownership of their stock. Analysts say the Muscat bourse is one of the best regulated in the Gulf.
Financial stocks have led this year's gains, with bank and investment stocks rising some 95 percent this year. Insurers are about 62 percent stronger and services stocks are 33 percent up.
"It is impossible to buy financial services shares, there just aren't any available," said one Muscat stock watcher.
Oman Securities Portfolio is some 400 percent up at 5.08 rials from 1.05 in January and Al-Ahlia Portfolio is almost 200 percent up at 10.30 rials from 3.47 on January 1.
But brokers said industrials were lagging behind, moving up only 25 percent since January. "It is not very comforting. Very few firms in the industrial sector have done as well," said one.
Some said the bourse had gone too far, too quickly. "It is frightening how fast the market has moved. It is heating up to a point where some fear it might correct," said one source.
"The market has already fully discounted some firms 1997 earnings and started discounting 1998 results," Rajnarayan said.
Analysts expect more gains, albeit with the odd dips. "The market isn't overvalued. It is still a good opportunity to buy," Nasser said, forecasting the index at 350 to 360 by year-end.

"The market was undervalued with a p.e. (price earnings ratio) of 10.5 compared to an average emerging market p.e. of 18. Now it is 14-15...There is no indication of a correction, but there are fewer buying opportunities," Rajnarayan said.

But some analysts questioned the sustainability of the sharp uptrend, cautioning that much of the liquidity came from bank borrowings. "Investors have been investing 10 times more than they normally would because they have taken bank loans in the hope that share prices will rise sharply," said a treasurer.
The Central Bank said this month it was keeping a close eye on banks to prevent them from granting big loans to customers specifically to fund initial public offering (IPO) purchases.

MSM executive president Mahmoud al-Jarwani has said he expects 20 to 25 new issues this year. He told Reuters recently that the IPOs might affect the secondary market and the index: "People may liquidate to go into the primary market."
